title: Pediatric Cardiology, Part 1: Chest pain, syncope, murmurs, heart failure

sections.title: Case: exertional chest pain with ST changes
notes: 15-year-old with chest pain **during exertion** (not before or after) and ST elevation: **anomalous coronary artery**, a major cause of sudden death in athletes.

sections.title: Chest pain: causes
notes: Most pediatric chest pain is **non-cardiac**. **Idiopathic** is most common (20 to 45%), reassure.

Cardiac (rare): coronary disease (**homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia**), **past Kawasaki** (aneurysm), anomalous coronary, **cocaine**, pericarditis, myocarditis, SVT, aortic stenosis, **Marfan dissection**, HCM, pulmonary hypertension.

sections.title: Red flags for cardiac chest pain
notes: Pain or **syncope with exertion or swimming**, exertional dyspnea, palpitations before the pain, family history of **HCM** or sudden death. Babies: poor feeding, fussiness.

sections.title: Non-cardiac chest pain
notes: **Musculoskeletal**: chest wall tenderness, NSAIDs and reassurance.
**Exercise-induced asthma**: chest tightness without cough, lungs clear in clinic. **Salbutamol before exercise** is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Also pneumonia, anxiety and stress, reflux, **sickle cell acute chest**.

sections.title: Vasovagal syncope
notes: Case: 13-year-old faints **while standing** after lightheadedness, nausea, pallor, sweating, recovers lying down: vasovagal. **Reassure, no ECG or labs**.
Fainting **lying down, while running or swimming** is abnormal.
Treatment: **more fluid and salt**. Recurrent: fludrocortisone, midodrine, beta blockers, pacemaker for documented bradycardia.

sections.title: Cardiac syncope: red flags and workup
notes: Causes: **HCM**, aortic stenosis, coronary anomalies, VT, complete heart block. Non-cardiac: seizure, hypoglycemia, psychogenic.

Red flags (refer to cardiology): palpitations, dyspnea or chest pain first, syncope **with exercise, swimming or supine**, **startle-triggered** (long QT), age under 10, heart disease, family history of cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, abnormal exam, **bradycardia**.
First test **ECG** (long QT, ventricular hypertrophy), then Holter or event monitor, echo if exam or ECG abnormal.

sections.title: Innocent murmur
notes: Case: 4-year-old, **1/6 low-pitched vibratory systolic** murmur at the left sternal border, **softer sitting up**: innocent (Still's) murmur.
Innocent murmurs: **always systolic**, grade 1 to 2, musical, louder supine, no radiation.
Mitral and tricuspid: stenosis is diastolic, regurgitation systolic. Aortic and pulmonary: stenosis systolic, regurgitation diastolic.

sections.title: How to listen and benign murmurs
notes: Listen supine then sitting, then the back. Grade 1 to 6, timing, location of maximum intensity, radiation, pitch.
**Peripheral pulmonary stenosis of the newborn**: soft systolic at the left upper sternal border, **radiates to both axillae and back**, gone by 3 to 6 months.
**Venous hum**: continuous, right infraclavicular, sitting up, **disappears lying down or with jugular pressure**.

sections.title: Pathologic murmurs
notes: Systolic ejection: **aortic stenosis** (right upper sternal border), pulmonary stenosis (left upper), **ASD** (left upper, flow), coarctation (left clavicle and back).
Holosystolic: **VSD** (harsh, left lower sternal border), mitral regurgitation (blowing, apex to left axilla), tricuspid regurgitation.
Early diastolic: aortic regurgitation (leaning forward). Mid-diastolic rumble: mitral stenosis.
Continuous: **PDA** (left infraclavicular, machinery), coronary fistula.

sections.title: Case: heart failure in Down syndrome
notes: 5-month-old with trisomy 21, RR 70, **clear lungs**, sats 85%, 3/6 holosystolic murmur, liver 4 cm: **heart failure** from a congenital defect (AV canal or VSD). Next step: **furosemide**.
**Tachypnea with clear lungs and a murmur**: think cardiac, not bronchiolitis. 40 to 50% of Down syndrome have heart disease.

sections.title: Heart failure: causes and presentation
notes: Left-to-right shunts (VSD, AV canal, PDA) present at **1 to 3 months** as pulmonary resistance falls. **Oxygen can make it worse**.
Low output: dilated cardiomyopathy, neonatal aortic stenosis or coarctation, restrictive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pericardial effusion, SVT.
Picture: poor growth, **sweating and tiring with feeds**, tachypnea, grunting, hepatomegaly, gallop. Older kids: exercise intolerance, abdominal pain.

sections.title: Heart failure: workup and treatment
notes: Pulse oximetry, chest x-ray, echo, **BNP**, troponin.
Treat the cause. **Diuretics (furosemide)** for overload, milrinone or nitroprusside, ACE inhibitors and beta blockers for remodelling.
